decisions.quote: Recently, a large meta-analysis has confirmed that the SNP rs190982 polymorphism within MEF2C on chromosome 5 acted as a protective factor for AD dementia (OR = 0.93, 95%CI = 0.90-0.95, P = 3.2×10 −8 ) in the Caucasian population [ 14 ]. Similarly, the association between the MEF2C gene rs190982 polymorphism and AD was also confirmed in a large Spanish sample (OR = 0.885, 95%CI = 0.811-0.966) [ 15 ]. Furthermore, another two studies replicated the association in China Han. Regretfully, they failed to reveal any association of rs190982 polymorphism in MEF2C gene with AD susceptibility in our Han Chinese cohort [ 16 , 17 ]. Here, we conducted a case-control study containing 2332 individuals to clarify whether the selected SNP on MEF2C gene has an association with LOAD in Northern Han Chinese population.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. The primary replication target of Tang et al. (2016) is the IGAP GWAS discovery of the protective MEF2C rs190982 association with late-onset Alzheimer's disease in 74,046 Caucasians reported by Lambert et al. (2013) [14], which is already represented by shipped row 1136 (10.1038/ng.2802) and singled out in both the Abstract ('identified to be related to late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) in Caucasians in a large meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS)') and the Discussion sample-size comparison ('Caucasian 74 046 vs. Chinese 4089'). Ruiz et al. (2014) [15] ('Follow-up of loci from the International Genomics of Alzheimer's Disease Project identifies TRIP4 as a novel susceptibility gene', 10.1038/tp.2014.2) is an earlier follow-up/replication of the IGAP loci in a Spanish sample, grouped in the Introduction with two prior Chinese replication studies [16, 17] ('Furthermore, another two studies replicated the association in China Han') and in Methods as one of the 'other reports on the associations between MEF2C (rs190982) and LOAD [ 15 – 17 ]' pooled with [14] in the secondary meta-analysis.

decisions.quote:
This study examined whether the cognitive asymmetry process would be replicated in 

the context of physical activity, using a high-powered design as in Francis et al. (2022).  
It should be noted that this study was originally designed to investigate whether 
exposure to weight stigma prevents the cognitive asymmetry process from occurring in people 
concerned about their weight. However, because we did not replicate the cognitive asymmetry 
process, this hypothesis was not testable, and only the cognitive asymmetry results are 
presented.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. The empirically retested original study is Cheval et al. (2017) (already represented by shipped row 2360, 10.1016/j.psychsport.2017.02.006), whose physical-activity primed lexical decision task, inclusion questionnaire, and mixed-effects analysis were preregistered (AsPredicted #52738) and re-run to test the hypothesized cognitive asymmetry interaction ('This pre-registered study aimed to replicate the cognitive asymmetry process in the physical activity domain found in Cheval et al. (2017)'; 'Contrary to our hypothesis that temptation-related primes should lead to faster recognition of goal-related target words, and that goal-related primes should not lead to faster recognition of temptation-related targets (asymmetrical activation pattern), the results revealed a non-significant Target x Prime interaction'). Francis et al. (2022) (10.1525/collabra.31030) is an earlier failed replication study in the academic context (testing Fishbach et al., 2003) cited for motivation, post-hoc sensitivity power analysis method (SIMR), and Discussion-section post-hoc consistency/extension of an unhypothesized main effect of Prime rather than an independently retested target.

decisions.quote:
Although burrowing is a relatively novel pain outcome measure, a few studies have reported decreased burrowing in rat models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain; importantly, burrowing deficits were reversed by known analgesics, suggesting a degree of predictive validity for this outcome measure.2,9,20,35,61,62
We hypothesise that by using a prospective multicentre design, the reliability of novel outcome measures can be efficiently and rapidly evaluated. As part of the IMI Europain collaboration (http://www.imieuropain.org), we investigated rat burrowing behaviour after induction of complete Freund adjuvant (CFA)-associated inflammation across 8 centres to assess the reliability of suppressed burrowing as a pain-related outcome measure.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. This IMI Europain multicentre validation study retests CFA-induced suppression of rat burrowing originally reported by Andrews et al. (2012) [2] (already represented by shipped row 182, 10.1016/j.ejpain.2011.07.012), from which the experimental protocol was taken ('Burrowing experiments were performed as previously described.2,62', where [62] is Rutten et al. 2014 in a knee-joint inflammation model). Gould et al. (2016) [20] ('Pharmacological characterization of intraplantar Complete Freund's Adjuvant-induced burrowing deficits', Behav Brain Res 2016;301:142–51) was published in 2016—after all 11 multicentre experiments in the present study were completed between June 2013 and September 2014 (Results 3.1)—by co-author A. Pekcec's Boehringer Ingelheim group, and is cited only in a six-reference background cluster [2,9,20,35,61,62] and Discussion remarks [2,20,62] on analgesic reversal (ibuprofen vs. gabapentin), which this non-pharmacological study did not test.

decisions.quote: Kleiman and Rule (2013) demonstrated that naive observers could categorize static images at above chance levels according to suicidality and that the faces of individuals who died by suicide were rated as more impulsive than control faces. We attempted to replicate these results with a larger sample and extended the original report by implementing a 2AFC paradigm that minimizes response bias.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. The blind target ('Kleiman and Rule', 2013, coded from an abstract-only OSF preprint record without a reference list) is already represented by shipped row 2147 (Kleiman & Rule, 10.1177/1948550612466115, 'Detecting Suicidality From Facial Appearance', Social Psychological and Personality Science, Vol. 4, Issue 4, pp. 453–460). Crossref metadata confirms that 2012 is the OnlineFirst publication year (November 16, 2012) and 2013 is the print issue year for the same original paper.

decisions.quote: Background: A study by White et al. found that population disease burden predicted preference for attractive politicians in U.S. congressional elections. Aim: We aimed to replicate this finding using data from the United Kingdom.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. The blind target (coded with year 2013 and empty authors/title/DOI because the supplied PeerJ Preprints source text is abstract-only and cites 'White et al ., Psych Sci 2013' in the title and 'White et al.' in the abstract without a reference list) is already represented by shipped row 2369 (White, Kenrick, & Neuberg, 2013, Psychological Science, 'Beauty at the Ballot Box', 10.1177/0956797613493642), which reports the exact U.S. congressional election disease-threat and candidate-attractiveness finding retested here.

decisions.quote: An association between a polymorphic ApaLI site within the porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD) gene and schizophrenia has been reported recently. In order to replicate this finding we examined the ApaLI RFLP, which is located in intron 1 of the PBGD gene, in 93 unrelated patients who met the DSM-III-R criteria for schizophrenia versus 74 unrelated controls. There were no significant differences between the groups in allele frequencies or genotype counts.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. The blind target has empty bibliographic fields solely because the supplied source text for Nöthen et al. (1993) is abstract-only and describes the recently reported association between the polymorphic ApaLI site in the porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD) gene and schizophrenia without printing a citation. That single retested original finding is already represented by shipped row 1510 (Sanders et al., January 1993, Schizophrenia Research, 'Association between genetic variation at the porphobilinogen deaminase gene and schizophrenia', 10.1016/0920-9964(93)90019-f).
